analysis.one_liner: Ends the exemption that lets farm employers pay no overtime, phasing in a 40-hour weekly overtime threshold.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 86 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in July 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end a decades-old carve-out that excludes farmworkers from overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Employers would have to pay time-and-a-half after 55 hours a week starting in 2024, stepping down to 40 hours by 2027 (later dates for farms with 25 or fewer employees), and agricultural workers would lose several other minimum wage and labor law exemptions. The bill was introduced on July 12, 2023, referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and never received any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers — about 2.5 million people who plant, tend, and harvest the country's food — would gain the same overtime pay and minimum wage protections nearly all other workers have had under the Fair Labor Standards Act since 1938. Many are paid hourly with no overtime after long weekly hours during harvest season; under the bill, hours beyond 55 a week in 2024, stepping down to 40 a week by 2027, would have to be paid at time-and-a-half, and agricultural workers would no longer be carved out of minimum wage and related protections, with later start dates for farms with 25 or fewer employees.

how_it_helps.text: Would give farmworkers overtime pay at one-and-a-half times their regular rate for hours above 55 a week in 2024, 50 in 2025, 45 in 2026, and 40 from 2027 onward, ending the FLSA's agricultural overtime exemption (repealing section 7(m)).
Would narrow the agricultural minimum wage exemption so it applies only to the employer's own immediate family members, extending minimum wage coverage to hired farmworkers.

Would strike several other Fair Labor Standards Act exemptions for agricultural labor, including exemptions from recordkeeping and related requirements, and conform the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act's small-farm threshold accordingly.
Would give farms with 25 or fewer employees more time to adjust, with the overtime and most other requirements starting in 2027 to 2030 for them, versus 2024 to 2027 for larger employers.

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers, especially fruit, vegetable, and other labor-intensive farm operations, would bear higher payroll costs for hours above the weekly threshold, and some of that cost would likely show up in food prices or in reduced hours for workers. Employers with 25 or fewer workers would get several extra years before the rules fully apply.

drawbacks.text: The added overtime cost would fall heavily on labor-intensive growers, who could respond by cutting workers' hours, hiring fewer people, speeding mechanization, or raising prices — meaning some of the intended benefit could be offset.

The phase-in is slow: workers would not see the full 40-hour overtime threshold until 2027 (or 2030 at small farms), and during harvest peaks growers could simply cap schedules at the threshold rather than pay overtime.

Critics of extending overtime to agriculture have long argued that seasonal harvest work and weather-dependent schedules make rigid weekly thresholds impractical for growers and could shrink take-home hours for workers who want long harvest weeks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward and long overdue on its face: farmworkers are the last major group still excluded from the federal overtime and minimum wage guarantees that other workers have had for over 80 years, and the bill closes those gaps with a phased schedule and slower timelines for small farms. The real costs are concentrated on growers, who would pay more for long harvest weeks and might respond with shorter hours, fewer jobs, or higher prices, and the bill offers no separate mechanism to cushion small farms beyond delay. The biggest honest caveat is not design but fate: the bill never moved at all, so none of these trade-offs were ever tested in a debate or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 12, 2023, and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — was ever taken on the bill in committee.
All 86 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers are better off: farmworkers remain exempt from federal overtime and several minimum wage rules, so labor costs stay where they were. The roughly 2.5 million farmworkers who would have gained overtime pay are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agricultural employers who keep paying no overtime

industries.industry: Labor-intensive agriculture (fruit, vegetable, dairy, and other crop and livestock employers)
industries.note: The bill would require these employers to pay time-and-a-half above a phased-in weekly threshold (55 hours in 2024 down to 40 by 2027) and remove their minimum wage and related exemptions, raising labor costs in a sector that has operated under the 1938 carve-outs for decades. Because the bill never advanced, their current cost structure continues unchanged.

industries.industry: Farm labor contractors and crew leaders
industries.note: Labor contractors who supply crews to growers are covered under the bill's removal of the man-days and related exemptions, so they too would face overtime obligations. As with growers, the bill's failure leaves their status quo intact.
